title: Report on Studying at Duke University
paragraphs: Looking back on my study abroad now, I think it was an intense experience that greatly changed my values. In gratitude to the people around me who supported me in every way, I would like to report on the content of my clerkships.

The first month was a clerkship in the rheumatology outpatient clinic. Everything was of course in English, and I was in an environment where I did not know my way around, so I struggled a great deal at first, but every day I was surprised by the various differences from Japan in medicine, culture, race and so on. From the local students I was working with, I learned that by proactively appealing for it I could be entrusted with higher-level work, so I made a special effort, including preparing presentations, to be entrusted with as much as possible. As a result, I came to be allowed to take the history and examine outpatients by myself, and I saw a little over 40 patients in this way, which I think was a very good experience. At the same time, I was full of gratitude for the generosity of people who willingly entrusted such work to a student who was not even a doctor, and moreover an international student with a language barrier.

The second month was a clerkship in cardiology, and I belonged to a team consisting of an attending, a resident and three students including me, and took on consult work every day. This clerkship, which began each morning with practice using a human body model, was very educational and stimulating. For a consult requested of the team, the student first takes the history and examines the patient, but naturally we were required to go as far as making the differential diagnosis and the treatment plan. And given the nature of cardiology, I often saw severe patients. So every time I was working on a consult, I was desperate and tense, feeling as though I would get a hole in my stomach. I also cannot forget the joy when, after I was entrusted with the consult of a patient who seemed about to die and gave my presentation, the plan I had come up with was adopted.

The third month was a clerkship in hematology and oncology, in which I was in charge of inpatients for a month. In terms of both physical and intellectual demands, it was the most intense month. This department starts with a morning conference at 6:30 a.m. Before that I needed to visit my own patients, grasp their condition and prepare my presentation, so I got up at 4:30 every day and went home at night by the university's late-night taxi. The mornings ended with rounds that took nearly 30 minutes per patient, so there was no time to catch my breath. In the afternoons I did clerkships at various facilities, including the bone marrow transplant center, the oncology clinic that had only been completed this year and was like a hotel, and a veterans' hospital, and I think it was very fulfilling. By this time I had also gotten used to English, and I think I was able to ask questions and learn on a par with what I would have done if I had done the same clerkship in Japanese.

What impressed me throughout was the doctors' attitude toward education. I was impressed that they had students take an active part in medical care and spared no effort to help them learn. I was also strongly impressed by the attitude of many doctors who always try to look up the latest information. I strongly want to become an educational doctor myself someday, and seeing so many role models, I keenly felt that to do so I need an attitude and effort of continually updating my knowledge however old I become.

Outside the clerkships, talking with international students from Taiwan and Sweden and with Duke students, at lunch conferences, in small gaps in the clerkships and sometimes even on weekends, is another of my memories of studying abroad. Talking in English about all sorts of things, from serious themes such as differences in the healthcare systems of their countries, the content of the morning's clerkship and what we had learned, to trivial jokes and girl talk, and laughing, being surprised and thinking together, I truly felt that I was studying abroad.

I am heartily grateful for the very valuable experiences I was given every day. I also think that my task from now on is to give back what I learned from the study abroad experience in some form. I would like to express my gratitude to the professors of Nagoya University who supported this study abroad, everyone in the Student Affairs Division and the International Exchange Office, the professors, students and staff I met at Duke, the Japanese doctors I met and who looked after me there, Fred and Jenny who kindly accepted me as a guest, my fellow exchange students with whom I studied and encouraged one another, and my parents who fully supported me at all times. Thank you very much.
